            </li>
          </ol>
        </nav>
        <div class="td-content">
          
          <h1>Contributing to Models</h1>
           <p><strong>Meshery Models are schema-driven.</strong> Model definitions, including their structure, metadata, and versioning, are defined by JSON Schemas in the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas"><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">meshery/schemas</code></a> repository. Before contributing to models, familiarize yourself with the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/tree/master/schemas/constructs/v1beta1/model">Model schema</a> and see <a href="/v0.8/project/contributing/contributing-schemas">Contributing to Schemas</a> for the development workflow.</p>

<h2 id="understanding-the-internals-of-mesherys-logical-object-model">Understanding the internals of Meshery’s logical object model</h2>

<p>Meshery uses a logical object model to describe the infrastructure and capabilities it manages in a consistent and extensible way.</p>

<h4 id="what-are-meshery-models">What Are Meshery Models?</h4>

<p>At the core of this system are <strong>Meshery Models</strong> — packages that define a specific type of infrastructure, application, or capability. These models include:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong><a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/components">Components</a></strong>: Individual parts of a system (e.g., services, databases).</li>
  <li><strong><a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/relationships">Relationships</a></strong>: How those parts interact.</li>
  <li><strong>Metadata</strong>: Visual and behavioral traits, such as icons or capabilities.</li>
</ul>

<p>Models can describe traditional technologies (like Kubernetes workloads), or more abstract entities (like annotations or diagrams).</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Learn more: <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/models">What are Meshery Models?</a></p>
</blockquote>

<h4 id="what-is-the-model-schema">What Is the Model Schema?</h4>

<p>Each model includes a set of entities (in the form of definitions) that Meshery can manage. Models are defined and versioned using the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/blob/master/schemas/constructs/openapi/meshmodels.yml">Model Schema</a>.</p>

<p>The schema defines the structure of the model, including the entities it contains, their relationships, and the properties they have. The schema also defines the version of the model and the version of the schema itself.</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>See <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/registry">Registry</a> to learn more about Meshery’s internal registry and how to use it.</p>
</blockquote>

<p><a href="/v0.8/assets/img/concepts/meshery-models.png"><img src="/assets/img/meshmodel/meshmodel-architecture.svg" alt="Model Entity Classification" /></a>
<em>Figure: Model Entity Classification</em></p>

<h2 id="meshery-entities-and-their-lifecycle">Meshery Entities and their Lifecycle</h2>

<p>This section aids in your understanding of the vernacular of Meshery’s internal object model and discusses the difference beteween schemas, definitions, declarations, and instances. The lifecycle of Meshery entities (components, relationships, policies) is represented by the following terms, which are used to describe the various stages of their lifecycle.</p>

<h3 id="schema">Schema</h3>

<p><strong>Schema</strong> <em>(static)</em> <strong>: the skeletal structure representing a logical view of the size, shape, characteristics of a construct.</strong></p>

<p>The schema represents the skeletal structure of an entity and provides a logical view of its size, shape, and characteristics. It defines the expected properties and attributes of the entity. The schema serves as a blueprint or template for creating instances of the entity. It is a static representation that defines the structure and properties but does not contain specific configuration values.</p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Schema example</h4>
<details><summary>Component schema excerpt</summary><pre> {
"$id": "https://schemas.meshery.io/component.json",
  "$schema": "&lt;http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#&gt;",
"description": "Components are the atomic units for designing infrastructure. Learn more at &lt;https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/components&gt;",
"required": [
"apiVersion",
"kind",
"schema",
"model"
],
"additionalProperties": false,
"type": "object",
"properties": {
"apiVersion": {
"type": "string",
"description": "API Version of the component."
},
"kind": {
"type": "string",
"description": "Kind of the component."
.
.
.

</pre></details> See <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas">github.com/meshery/schemas</a> for more details.
</div>

<h3 id="definition">Definition</h3>

<p><strong>Definition</strong> <em>(static)</em> <strong>: An implementation of the Schema containing an outline of the specific attributes of a given, unconfigured entity.</strong></p>

<p>A definition is an implementation of the schema. It contains specific configurations and values for the entity at hand. The definition provides the actual configuration details for a specific instance of the entity. It is static because it is created based on the schema but does not change once created. The definition is used to instantiate declarations of the entity.</p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Definition example</h4>
a generic, unconfigured Kubernetes Pod.
</div>

<h3 id="declaration">Declaration</h3>

<p><strong>Declaration</strong> <em>(static)</em> <strong>: - A configured entity with detailed intentions of a given Definition.</strong></p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Declaration example</h4>
NGINX container as a Kubernetes Pod with port 443 and SSL termination.
</div>

<h3 id="instance">Instance</h3>

<p><strong>Instance</strong> <em>(dynamic)</em> <strong>: A realized entity (deployed/discovered); An instantiation of the declaration.</strong></p>

<p>An <em>instance</em> represents a realized entity. An <em>instance</em> is a dynamic representation that corresponds to a deployed or discovered instantiation of a <em>declaration</em>. An <em>instance</em> is created based on its corresponding <em>definition</em> and represents an actual running or deployed version of the entity within the environment.</p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Instance example</h4>
NGINX-as234z2 pod running in a cluster as a Kubernetes Pod with port 443 and SSL termination.
</div>

<h3 id="capabilities">Capabilities</h3>

<p><strong>Capabilities</strong>: Capabilities are used to describe the operations that a model supports.</p>

<p>Models use <strong>capabilities</strong> to describe the operations which they support, such as styling, configurations, interactions, and runtime behavior. Entities may define a broad array of capabilities, which are in turn dynamically interpreted by Meshery for full lifecycle management.</p>

<p>To simplify the assignment of these capabilities, Meshery organizes these capabilities into reusable and assignable sets, such as:</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Default Set:</strong>
A foundational set covering configuration (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Workload Configuration</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Labels and Annotations</code>), UI interaction (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Styling</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Change Shape</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Compound Drag and Drop</code>), and component introspection (<code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Relationships</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Json Schema</code>).</li>
  <li><strong>Shapes:</strong>
Visual components with layout and appearance-related capabilities. Includes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Styling</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Change Shape</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Compound Drag and Drop</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Body Text</code>.</li>
  <li><strong>Comment:</strong>
Annotation-like elements with light interaction. Similar to <strong>Shapes</strong>, but focused on non-functional overlays.</li>
  <li><strong>Ghost:</strong>
Lightweight visual components with minimal styling. Typically lacks body text or complex interactions.</li>
  <li><strong>Shapes without Text:</strong>
Variant of <strong>Shapes</strong>, omitting <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Body Text</code> to support simpler block structures.</li>
  <li><strong>Component with Logging and Terminal Session Support:</strong>
Extends the Default set with operational capabilities like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Performance Test</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Interactive Terminal</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Stream Logs</code>.</li>
  <li><strong>Container Alias:</strong>
Alias components that simulate real workloads, combining configuration, view, and operational capabilities.</li>
</ul>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Capabilities Schema example</h4>
<details><summary>Capabilities schema excerpt</summary><pre> {
"$id": "https://schemas.meshery.io/capability.json",
"$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
"description": "Meshery manages entities in accordance with their specific capabilities. This field explicitly identifies those capabilities largely by what actions a given component supports; e.g. metric-scrape, sub-interface, and so on. This field is extensible. Entities may define a broad array of capabilities, which are in-turn dynamically interpretted by Meshery for full lifecycle management.",
"additionalProperties": false,
"type": "object",
"required":
.
...
.
"kind": {
"description": "Top-level categorization of the capability",
"additionalProperties": false,
"anyOf": [
{
"const": "action",
"description": "For capabilities related to executing actions on entities. Example: initiate log streaming on a Pod. Example: initiate deployment of a component."
},
{
"const": "mutate",
"description": "For capabilities related to mutating an entity. Example: the ability to change the configuration of a component."
},
.
.
.

</pre></details> See <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/blob/master/typescript/constructs/v1alpha1/capability/CapabilityOpenApiSchema.ts">Capabilities Schema</a> for more details.
</div>

<h3 id="importing-and-creating-models">Importing and Creating Models</h3>

<p>Models can be created from scratch or imported using either the Meshery UI or the Meshery CLI.<br />
To learn more, see the detailed guides on <a href="/v0.8/guides/configuration-management/importing-models">Importing Models</a> and <a href="/v0.8/guides/configuration-management/creating-models">Creating Models</a>.</p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Use <strong>Create</strong> if you’re starting from scratch. Use <strong>Import</strong> if you already have model definitions (e.g., JSON, CSV, tar).</p>
</blockquote>

<h3 id="model-generation-from-schemas">Model Generation from Schemas</h3>

<p>Meshery automatically generates models and components by parsing schemas from various sources. While <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/api-extension/custom-resources/">Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)</a> are a common source, Meshery can create components from any valid schema definition.</p>

<h4 id="component-grouping-into-models">Component Grouping into Models</h4>

<p>When generating components, Meshery processes input schemas and automatically organizes them into <strong>Models</strong>. This grouping process logically binds related components together based on their source.</p>

<p><strong>Source-Based Grouping:</strong><br />
Components are grouped based on their origin—such as a specific GitHub repository, Helm chart, or Kubernetes cluster. For example:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Importing a Helm chart for Prometheus from ArtifactHub creates a “Prometheus” Model containing all resources defined in that chart (Services, Deployments, ConfigMaps, etc.) as components</li>
  <li>Connecting to a Kubernetes cluster creates a “Kubernetes” Model containing all discovered CRDs as components</li>
  <li>Importing from a GitHub repository creates a model named after the repository</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Metadata Preservation:</strong><br />
For Kubernetes CRDs, the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">spec.group</code> field is extracted and stored as part of each component’s API version (e.g., <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">networking.k8s.io/v1</code>). This metadata is preserved but does not determine model assignment for direct imports.</p>

<h4 id="component-generation-behavior">Component Generation Behavior</h4>

<p>When Meshery processes schemas:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>Parsing</strong>: The source is parsed to extract schema specifications for every entity.</li>
  <li><strong>Component Creation</strong>: A component definition is generated for each entity, capturing its kind, version, and schema.</li>
  <li><strong>Model Assignment</strong>: Components are automatically assigned to a Model based on their source context.</li>
  <li><strong>Registration</strong>: Components are registered in Meshery’s <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/registry">Registry</a> under their respective model.</li>
  <li><strong>Enrichment</strong>: Components inherit default properties from their model and can be further customized.</li>
</ol>

<p>This automatic grouping allows you to manage related resources as cohesive units within Meshery designs.</p>

<h4 id="advanced-grouping-by-api-group-csv-imports">Advanced: Grouping by API Group (CSV Imports)</h4>

<p>When importing models via CSV or Google Spreadsheet, you can optionally specify a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">group</code> field to filter which CRDs are included based on their <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">spec.group</code> value. This filtering capability is <strong>specific to CSV/spreadsheet imports</strong> and is not available for direct imports from GitHub repositories, ArtifactHub packages, or live Kubernetes clusters.</p>

<p><strong>How Group Filtering Works:</strong></p>

<p>During CSV import, if you specify a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">group</code> value in your model definition, Meshery will only process CRDs whose <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">spec.group</code> field matches the specified value. This allows you to create focused models containing only components from a specific Kubernetes API group.</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>With a group specified</strong>: Only CRDs matching the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">spec.group</code> value are processed</li>
  <li><strong>Without a group specified</strong> (empty field): All CRDs from the source are processed</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Example:</strong></p>

<p>In the CRD below, the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">spec.group</code> field has the value <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">cloudquota.cnrm.cloud.google.com</code>:</p>

<pre class="codeblock-pre" style="font-size: 1.75rem !important;">
<div class="codeblock">
<code class="clipboardjs">apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  annotations:
    cnrm.cloud.google.com/version: 1.140.0
  name: apiquotaadjustersettings.cloudquota.cnrm.cloud.google.com
spec:
  group: cloudquota.cnrm.cloud.google.com # API group used for filtering
  names:
    kind: APIQuotaAdjusterSettings
    plural: apiquotaadjustersettings
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
    - name: v1beta1
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          properties:
            apiVersion:
              type: string
            kind:
              type: string


  </code>
</div>
</pre>
<p><strong>CSV Model Definition Example:</strong></p>

<pre><code class="language-csv">model,group,category,modelDisplayName,registrant
gcp-cloudquota,cloudquota.cnrm.cloud.google.com,Cloud Native Network,GCP Cloud Quota,artifacthub
</code></pre>

<p>When this CSV is imported with associated CRD files, only CRDs from the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">cloudquota.cnrm.cloud.google.com</code> API group will be included as components in the “gcp-cloudquota” model.</p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">CSV Import Only</h4>
Group filtering is only available when importing via CSV or Google Spreadsheet. For all other import methods (GitHub repositories, ArtifactHub/Helm packages, or live Kubernetes clusters), all available resources are processed and organized into models based on their source.
</div>

<p><strong>When to Use Group Filtering:</strong></p>

<p>Group filtering is useful when:</p>

<ul>
  <li>You want to create separate models for different API groups from the same source</li>
  <li>You’re working with a large collection of CRDs and need to organize them by Kubernetes API group</li>
  <li>You need fine-grained control over which CRDs are included in a specific model</li>
</ul>

<p>For most use cases, the automatic source-based grouping is sufficient and requires no additional configuration.</p>

<h3 id="post-model-generation">Post Model Generation</h3>

<p>During model generation, corresponding components are created. Next step is to enrich these component details and define their capabilities and relationships.</p>

<ol>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Enrich Component Details</strong>
When a Component is initially generated, a new Component definition is created with default properties (e.g. colors, icons, capabilities, etc.), some of which are inherited from their respective Model.</p>

    <ul>
      <li>
        <p><strong>1.1. Customize Shapes and Colors</strong></p>

        <ul>
          <li>Default shape for new components is a circle</li>
          <li>Consider enriching components’ details based on what they represent</li>
          <li>Reference Cytoscape <a href="https://js.cytoscape.org/demos/node-types/">node types</a> for possible shapes</li>
          <li>Example: Use a pentagon shape to represent a Deployment</li>
          <li>Know more about <a href="https://docs.meshery.io/guides/configuration-management/identifying-components">components shapes and colors</a></li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p><strong>1.2. Customize Icons</strong></p>

        <ul>
          <li>Components inherit the icon (colored and white SVGs) of their respective Model by default</li>
          <li>Propose specific icons best suited to visually represent each component</li>
          <li>Example: Use a skull icon for a DaemonSet</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p><strong>1.3. Review Capabilities</strong></p>
        <ul>
          <li>Review and confirm assigned capabilities</li>
          <li>Modify capabilities as needed</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
    </ul>

    <p>See the <a href="/v0.8/project/contributing/contributing-components">Contributing to Components</a> for detailed instructions.</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Identify Relationships</strong></p>

    <ul>
      <li>
        <p><strong>2.1. Review Available Types</strong>
Review and familiarize yourself with the predefined relationship kinds, types, and subtypes. See <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/relationships">“Relationships logical concepts”</a></p>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p><strong>2.2. Map Component Relationships</strong></p>

        <ul>
          <li>Identify appropriate relationships for your new components</li>
          <li>Consider how components relate to others within the same model</li>
          <li>Consider relationships with components in other models</li>
        </ul>
      </li>
      <li>
        <p><strong>2.3. Create Definitions</strong>
Codify the relationships you have identified into a Relationship Definition</p>
      </li>
    </ul>

    <p>See the <a href="/v0.8/project/contributing/contributing-relationships">Contributing to Relationships</a> for detailed instructions.</p>
  </li>
</ol>

<h2 id="next-steps">Next Steps</h2>

<p>The Meshery team is currently working on the following:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Extending the model to support additional entities</li>
  <li>Improving the tooling for working with models</li>
  <li>Defining relationships between components and embedding those policies within models</li>
</ul>

<p>We encourage you to get involved in the development of Meshery Models and to share your feedback!</p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Meshery Models are extensible</h4>
Meshery Models are designed to be extensible, allowing you to define new components as needed. If you have an idea for a new component, please create one and share it with the Meshery community.
</div>

<script>
$(document).ready(function() {

    var toc = $('#TOC');

    // Select each header
    sections = $('.td-content h1');
        $.each(sections, function(idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if(!section.hasClass('noTOC')){
               var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
              var parent = $("#" + div_id)
              var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text +'">' + div_text +'</a></li>';
              $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            // Add section code to subnavigation
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil("h1");
            $.each(contenders, function(idx, contender){
               if( !$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && ($(contender).is('h2') || $(contender).is('h3')) ) {
                   var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                   var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                   var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text +'">' + contender_text +'</a></li>';
                   children.append(content);
                }
             })
             $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        //added 'selected' tag to the first element of toc
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function(e){
          // Detect how far are we from the top of the page
          let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
          // Loop through every navigation menu item
          $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {       
              if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
              // Remove 'selected' from previously highlighted menu items
              $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
              // Highlight the current menu item by adding 'selected' class
              $(this).addClass('selected');
          }
          if($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
            $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
              $(this).addClass('selected');
          }
        });
      })
      // Smooth scroll to target section when clicking on TOC link
      $('a[href^="#"]').on('click', function(event) {
        event.preventDefault();
        var target = $(this.hash);
        if (target.length) {
          $('html, body').animate({
          scrollTop: target.offset().top - 115
          }, 1000);
        }
      });
    });
</script>

        <div class="td-content">
          
          <h1>Contributing to Meshery Policies</h1>
           <h2 id="background">Background</h2>
<p>Meshery has a built-in policy engine, based on <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/">Open Policy Agent (OPA)</a>. Meshery uses the <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/policy-language/">Rego</a> query language to create these <a href="https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/policies">policies</a>.</p>

<h2 id="prerequisites">Prerequisites</h2>
<p>To start contributing to Meshery Policy Engine, make sure you have <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/#running-opa">OPA CLI</a> installed on your system. You will also need to clone the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/">Meshery Server</a> project from Github.</p>

<h2 id="components-of-meshery-policy-engine">Components of Meshery Policy Engine</h2>

<p>Rego policies are the declarative logic behind the policy engine. These policies define how the underlying engine understands relationships within Meshery Designs. Rego policies can be found <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/tree/master/server/meshmodel/meshery-core/0.7.2/v1.0.0/policies">here</a> in the Meshery Github repository.</p>

<p>Currently the Rego policies are invoked from the Go code in Meshery Server. This requires configuring the OPA context as seen <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshkit/blob/master/models/meshmodel/core/policies/rego_policy_relationship.go">here</a>.</p>

<p>The Meshery Policy Engine is invoked by calling the <a href="https://docs.meshery.io/reference/rest-apis#api-meshmodels-relationships-evaluate">evaluation endpoint</a>. This endpoint is passed a Meshery Design in JSON which it passes to the Meshery Policy Engine for validation.</p>

<h2 id="working-with-meshery-policy-engine">Working with Meshery Policy Engine</h2>

<p>Working with the Meshery Policy Engine can feel complex because of the large number of different relationships a Meshery Design might contain. Contributors must then be careful to test any changes thoroughly to avoid unexpected results. When working with the Rego policies themselves it makes testing and development easier to be able to test the policies directly without running the entire Meshery Server. When working on the policies keep the following in mind:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Since we will be running these policies using the OPA CLI directly without the Go bootstrap code we need to provide the necessary context for the policy engine. This means providing a data structure containing the valid Meshery Relationships the policy engine will evaluate against.</li>
  <li>The input to the policy engine is a Meshery Design as a JSON data structure. When testing the Meshery Policy Engine you will need to provide this design as input. If you are working on a bug you will need to get the design from the issue or directly from the individual who reported the bug.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="executing-opa">Executing OPA</h2>

<p>You can evaluate the Rego policies against test data stored in the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">policies/test</code> folder:</p>

<pre class="codeblock-pre" style="font-size: 1.75rem !important;">
<div class="codeblock">
<code class="clipboardjs">make rego-eval</code>
</div>
</pre>

               var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
              var parent = $("#" + div_id)
              var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text +'">' + div_text +'</a></li>';
              $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            // Add section code to subnavigation
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil("h1");
            $.each(contenders, function(idx, contender){
               if( !$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && ($(contender).is('h2') || $(contender).is('h3')) ) {
                   var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                   var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                   var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text +'">' + contender_text +'</a></li>';
                   children.append(content);

             })
             $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);

              // Highlight the current menu item by adding 'selected' class

              $(this).addClass('selected');

        <div class="td-content">
          
          <h1>Contributing to Model Relationships</h1>
           <p><strong>Relationships follow a schema-defined structure.</strong> The <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/tree/master/schemas/constructs/v1alpha3/relationship">Relationship schema</a> specifies how relationships between components are expressed. Refer to the schema when defining new relationship types or selectors. See <a href="/v0.8/project/contributing/contributing-schemas">Contributing to Schemas</a> for details.</p>

<p><a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/relationships">Relationships</a> within <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/models">Models</a> play a crucial role in establishing concrete visualisations of efficient data flow between different components of Meshery. These are used to classify the nature of interaction between one or more interconnected <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/components">Components</a>.</p>

<h2 id="overview-of-steps-to-create-relationships">Overview of Steps to Create Relationships</h2>

<p><strong>Prework:</strong></p>

<ol>
  <li><a href="#relationship-identification">Relationship Identification</a></li>
  <li><a href="#relationship-visualizations">Relationship Classification</a></li>
</ol>

<p><strong>Development:</strong></p>
<ol>
  <li><a href="#relationship-definitions">Relationship Definition</a></li>
  <li><a href="#relationship-scopes">Relationship Scopes</a></li>
</ol>

<p><strong>Postwork:</strong></p>
<ol>
  <li><a href="#relationship-testing">Relationship Testing</a></li>
  <li><a href="#relationship-contribution">Relationship Contribution</a></li>
</ol>

<h2 id="prework">Prework</h2>

<p><a id="relationship-identification"></a></p>

<h3 id="1-characterize-the-relationship-and-any-specific-constraints">1. Characterize the relationship and any specific constraints</h3>

<p>Using your domain expertise, define the qualities of this new relationship. Identify and qualify any specific constraints to be enforced between one or more specific components within the same or different models. Let’s take an example to understand this better.</p>

<p>For example, you might know that a Kubernetes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Service</code> can have a network-based relatinship with a Kubernetes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pod</code>. To codify this relationship, you would define the relationship as a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind: edge</code> relationship with a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type: network</code>.</p>

<details close="">
<summary>Relationship Example</summary>
<pre><code class="language-yaml highlighter-rouge">
{
  "schemaVersion": "core.meshery.io/v1alpha2",
  "kind": "edge",
  "type": "network",
  "version": "v1.0.0",
  "metadata": {"description": "A relationship that defines network edges between components."}
  selector: [{
      "allow": {
         "from": [
            {
               "kind": "Service",
               "model": "kubernetes"
            }
         ],
         "to": [
            {
               "kind": "Pod",
               "model": "kubernetes"
            }
         ]
      },
      "deny": {}
   }]

</code></pre>
</details>

<p>You might <em>also</em> know that this relationship is constrained by the presence of a Kubernetes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Deployment</code> as the parent of the Kubernetes <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pod</code>. This constraint would be codified in the relationship definition by including the <code>deny</code> function in your selector.</p>

<details close="">
<summary>Example Relationship with Constraints</summary>
<pre><code class="language-yaml highlighter-rouge">
selector: [
   {
      "allow": {
         "from": [
            {
               "kind": "Service",
               "model": "kubernetes"
            }
         ],
         "to": [
            {
               "kind": "Pod",
               "model": "kubernetes"
            }
         ]
      },
      "deny": {
         "from": [
            {
               "kind": "Service",
               "model": "kubernetes"
            }
         ],
         "to": [
            {
               "kind": "Pod",
               "model": "kubernetes",
               "parent": "Deployment"
            }
         ]
      }
   }
]
</code></pre>
</details>

<p>Codify relationships leveraging your domain expertise. In this example, the relationship between the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Service</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pod</code> components in the Kubernetes model is defined with appropriate consideration of surrounding constraints (e.g. presence of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Deployment</code>).</p>

<h4 id="understand-relationship-classifications">Understand Relationship Classifications</h4>

<p>Relationships can be classified into three main categories:</p>

<ol>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Hierarchical</strong> relationships involve either an ancestral connection of the components i.e. the creation/ deletion of a Component higher up affects the existence of the Components below in the lineage or a connection that involves the inheritance of features from one Component to the other.</p>

    <ol>
      <li><strong>Parent</strong>: A parent-child relationship implies the requirement of the parent component before the child component can be created. For example, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Namespace</code> in Kubernetes can be a parent of <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pods</code> within that namespace. The namespace must exist before creating pods within it.</li>
      <li><strong>Inventory</strong>: A hierarchical inventory relationship implies the configuration of a(parent) component is patched with the configuration of other (child) component. For example, Wasm filters can inherit features and functionalities from Envoy filters. This can be used to build on existing functionalities provided by Envoy filters and further extend them using Wasm filters. It enables a modular and scalable approach to customize the behavior of the proxy while maintaining a clear hierarchy of features.</li>
    </ol>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Edge</strong> relationships indicate the possibility of traffic flow between two components. They enable communication and interaction between different Components within the system.</p>

    <ol>
      <li><strong>Mount</strong>: This subtype addresses the storage and access possibility between involved components. For example, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">PersistentVolume</code> can be mounted to a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pod</code> to provide persistent storage for the pod’s data.</li>
      <li><strong>Network</strong>: This deals with IP addresses and DNS names and provides stable endpoints for communication. For example, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Service</code> provides a stable endpoint for accessing multiple replicas of a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Deployment</code>.</li>
      <li><strong>Firewall</strong>: This acts as an intermediary for communications which include standard networking protocols like TCP and UDP. It can enforce network policies to control traffic between components. For example, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">NetworkPolicy</code> can be used to manage the traffic flow between different <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Pods</code> in the cluster.</li>
      <li><strong>Permission</strong>: This defines the permissions for components if they can have a possible relationship with other Components. It ensures that only authorized Components can interact with each other. For example, a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Role</code> can define permissions for Components to access specific resources.</li>
    </ol>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p><strong>Sibling</strong> relationships represent connections between components that are at the same hierarchical level or share a common parent. Siblings can have the same or similar functionalities or may interact with each other in specific ways. These relationships facilitate communication and cooperation between components that are in the same group or category. For example, a Service and a Pod in Kubernetes are siblings as they share a common parent and are at the same hierarchical level.</p>
  </li>
</ol>

<p><a id="relationship-visualizations"></a></p>

<p>Once selected, note the relationship’s <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">subtype</code> of your selected visualization. Alternatively, if an existing visualization does not seem appropriate for the relationship, please propose a new visualization at-will. Simply use the whiteboard feature of Meshery’s extensions to sketch out the relationship and propose it as a new visualization.</p>

<h2 id="development">Development</h2>

<p><a id="relationship-definitions"></a></p>

<h3 id="3-create-a-relationship-definition-as-a-json-file">3. Create a Relationship Definition as a JSON file</h3>

<p>Create a relationship definition as a JSON file, placing this new definition file into its respective model folder (see <a href="./contributing-models">Contributing to Models</a>). Relationship definition files are commonly named  <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">relationships.yaml</code> as a convention, however, this name is not required. A model may include any number of relationship definitions. Include the following attributes in your relationship definition:</p>

<ul>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind</code>: The genre of relationship (e.g., hierarchical, edge, sibling).</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type</code>: The augmentative category of the relationship (e.g., binding, non-binding, inventory).</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">subType</code>: The specific representative visual paradigm (e.g., parent, mount, network, wallet, badge).</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">selectors</code>: The scope of the relationship, including the components involved and any constraints. Selector specify to which component(s) the relationship applies or does not apply (think of in terms of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AND</code> operators in a query). Selector Sets are used to combine multiple selectors for more granular control over the logic used when matchmaking (establishing a relationship) between components (think of in terms of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">OR</code> operators in a query).</li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code>: Name of the policy or policies (Open Policy Agent rego file(s)) to invoke for relationship evaluation. Identify an existing OPA policy as the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code> suitable to the relationship. If no policy exists, propose a new policy (rego). <em>(rarely necessary)</em> Create a new policy for the evaluation of your relationship using Rego. <em>This step is only necessary and can typically be skipped. Contact a maintainer if the relationship requires a new policy to evaluate the relationship.</em></li>
  <li><code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">description</code>: A characterization of the relationship, its purpose, and any constraints or considerations of its application.</li>
</ul>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Use Existing Relationships as Examples</h4>
Browse the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/tree/master/server/meshmodel">existing relationships in the Meshery repository</a> to find examples of how to existing relationships, using them as a template. Alternatively, you can review a prior pull request as an example as well, for example <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/pull/9880/files">PR #9880</a>.
</div>

<p><a class="anchorjs-link" id="relationship-scopes"></a></p>

<h3 id="4-configuring-the-scope-of-relationships">4. Configuring the Scope of Relationships</h3>

<p>The extent to which a relationship affects components within a model or beyond a model is defined and controlled using scopes. Scopes exist at two levels in Meshery relationships.</p>

<h4 id="global-scope">Global Scope</h4>

<p>Global scope is defined using the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">model</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version</code> attributes in the relationship definition.</p>

<p>Relationships can be confined to a specific model, a specific model version, or can be allowed to affect all models. The relationship schema has a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">model</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version</code> attribute which facilitates this control. For example, if the model is specified as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">aws-ec2-controller</code>, the relationship will work for those components that belong to the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">aws-ec2-controller</code> model.</p>

<h4 id="local-scope">Local Scope</h4>

<p>Local scope is defined and controlled via <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">selectors</code> attributes in the relationship definition.</p>

<p>Relationship selectors refine the scope of applicability the relationship. It is the details included within the Selector that determines whether there is a match and relationship to be formed. These details include which models and components are involved in the relationship and any constraints in its formation. Selector specify to which component(s) the relationship applies or does not apply (think of in terms of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">AND</code> operators in a query). Selector Sets are used to combine multiple selectors for more granular control over the logic used when matchmaking (establishing a relationship) between components (think of in terms of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">OR</code> operators in a query).</p>

<!-- @leecalcote: The following needs rewritten using Selector Sets, @MUzairS15 -->

<p>Selectors are structured as an array wherein each entry comprises a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> (self) property and a <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">to</code> (others) property. The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">to</code> combined with the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">allow</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">deny</code> properties delineate between components involved in a particular relationship. These entries define the constraints necessary for the existence of a relationship, thus scoping a relationship. Each item in the selector uniquely defines a relation between the components listed. i.e. <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">to</code> fields are evaluated within the context of the selector.</p>

<p>Only the components within the same selector relate to each other via 1:many kind of relation between components listed inside the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">to</code> field. i.e. Each object inside the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> relates to each item inside the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">two</code> field within a particular selector.</p>

<p>When defining relationships that involve a large number of combinations between <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">to</code>, selectors sets provide a mechanism to organize and manage these relationships. This prevents the need for crafting complex deny attributes and facilitates easier maintenance. Use of selector sets enhances flexibility and reusability in the definition and configuration of relationships among components.</p>

<p><em>Note: When defining Hierarchical relationships, remember that the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">from</code> field represents the child component, while the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">to</code> field represents the parent component.</em></p>

<details close="">
<summary>Relationship Selector Example</summary>


<figure class="highlight"><pre><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span class="na">selector</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="pi">[</span>
   <span class="pi">{</span>
      <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">allow"</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="pi">{</span>
         <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">from"</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="pi">[</span>
            <span class="pi">{</span>
               <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">kind"</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">WASMFilter"</span><span class="pi">,</span>
               <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">model"</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">istio-base"</span><span class="pi">,</span>
               <span class="s2">"</span><span class="s">patch"</span><span class="pi">:</span> <span class="pi">{</span>

The `selector` defined for the relationship between `WasmFilter` and `EnvoyFilter` components (the first item in the array) is entirely independent of the `selector` identified for the relationship between `ConfigMap` and `Deployment` components. This ensures independence in how these components relate to each other while still permitting similar types of relationships.

This example relationship demonstrates how the `WASMFilter` and `EBPFFilter` components identified in `from` relate to other `EnvoyFilter` `WASMPlugin` components identified in `to` selector. Similarly, `ConfigMap` component identified in the `from` selector corresponds to each `Deployment`, `StatefulSet`, and so on component identified in the `to` selector.

</details>

<h4 id="understanding-relationship-policies-and-their-evaluation">Understanding Relationship Policies and their Evaluation</h4>

<p>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code> property in your relationship definition is used to identity the name of the policy to be used by Meshery’s evaluation engine. Meshery embeds Open Policy Agent as it’s policy engine</p>

<p><strong>How should you determine the value for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code></strong></p>

<p>All relationship definitions are backed by OPA policies and each relationship depends on their <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">subType</code> in order to be properly evaluated. Which evaluation policy or set of policies used during the evaluation moment is defined by the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code> property, which follows the naming convention of combining each of their  <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">subType</code>  properties with an underscore and the word “_relationship”, like so: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind_type_subtype_relationship</code>.</p>

<p>So, for example, if you are defining or updating a relationship definition with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind: edge</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">type: network</code>, the value for the attribute <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code> should be <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">edge_network_relationship</code>.</p>

<p>Each policy has a set of evaluation rules defined and the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code> attribute corresponds to the main rule defined inside the policy, during the policy eval the results are collected from this rule.</p>

<h2 id="postwork">Postwork</h2>

<p><a id="relationship-testing"></a></p>

<h4 id="relationship-authoring-best-practices-and-considerations">Relationship Authoring Best Practices and Considerations</h4>

<h5 id="general">General</h5>

<ol>
  <li>Use camelCasing as the formatting convention.</li>
</ol>

<h5 id="scoping">Scoping</h5>

<ol>
  <li>To configure a relationship to be applied across models, ensure the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">model</code> property for those relationships is set to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">*</code>, to limit the relationships to a specific model, specify the correct <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">model</code>(case sensitive).</li>
  <li>To configure a relationship to be applied across all versions of a particular model, ensure the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version</code> property for those relationships is set to <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">*</code>, to limit the relationships to a specific version of a model, specify the correct model version.</li>
  <li>Specify <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version</code> property as a regex to ensure relationships are applied to a subset of versions of a model.</li>
</ol>

<h5 id="actions">Actions</h5>

<ol>
  <li>If a path <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">mutatedRef/mutatorRef</code> contains more than one array path then only the first array position can be specified as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">\_</code> for others explicitly mention them as 0</li>
  <li>Currently <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">mutatedRef</code> doesn’t support having an array.</li>
</ol>

<h5 id="matching">Matching</h5>

<ol>
  <li>Targets of a Relationship can be specific Components or entire Models.</li>
  <li>Values for propoerties like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version</code>, and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">model</code> are case-sensitive.</li>
  <li>Absence of a property in the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">selector</code> is interpretted as the wildcard <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">*</code>.
    <ul>
      <li>For example, a selector with <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">kind: Pod</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">Model: Kubernetes</code>, and the absence of the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version</code> property would be interpretted as <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">version: *</code>, which
means that all the versions of the Kubernetes Pod resource (k8s.io/v1/betav2) will match the selector.</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>The <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">evaluationQuery</code> property determines the OPA policy to invoke for relationship evaluation, specify the correct rego query.</li>
</ol>

<h5 id="conflicts">Conflicts</h5>

<ol>
  <li>Ensure that the <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">deny</code> selectors and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">allow</code> selectors do not conflict with each other i.e. relations are not getting overlapped for <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">allow</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">deny</code> selectors.</li>
  <li>In the event of conflicting Relationship Definitions, the union between them is taken.
    <ul>
      <li>If we have two Relationships, one from (Component A) to (Component B and Component F), and another
from (Component A) to (Component B and Component C), then it is similar to having a Relationship
from Component A to Component B, C and F</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>In the event of an overlapping set of complementary Relationship Definitions, Union.</li>
  <li>In the event of an overlapping set of conflicting Relationship Definitions, no relationship type (Kind) is inherently more important than the next one, so will not be any case of conflict.</li>
</ol>

<p><a class="anchorjs-link" id="relationship-contribution"></a></p>

<h4 id="4-contribute-your-relationship-to-the-meshery-project">4. Contribute your relationship to the Meshery project</h4>

<p>Submit a pull request to the Meshery repository with your new relationship definition, so that all users can benefit from the relationship(s) you have defined.</p>

<p>Keeping your relationship definition in a separate file allows for easier management and review of the relationship(s) you have defined.</p>

<div class="alert alert-info">
<h4 class="alert-heading">Keeping your custom Relationships private</h4>
Alternatively, if you would like to keep the relatioship definition private, you can bundle your relatinship(s) in a custom model, import the custom model into your Meshery deployment. Your private relationship definition(s) will be registered in your Meshery Server's <a href="/v0.8/concepts/logical/registry">registry</a> and available for use within your Meshery deployment.
</div>

<p>For more information refer - <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/16z5hA8qVfSq885of9LXFUVvfom-hQXr-6oTD_GgoFmk/edit">Model - Construct Models in Meshery</a></p>

<script>
$(document).ready(function() {

    var toc = $('#TOC');

    // Select each header
    sections = $('.td-content h1');
        $.each(sections, function(idx, v) {
            section = $(v);
            var div_id = $(section).attr('id');
            if(!section.hasClass('noTOC')){
               var div_text = section.text().split('¶')[0];
              var parent = $("#" + div_id)
              var content = '<li id="link_' + div_id + '" class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + div_id + '" title="' + div_text +'">' + div_text +'</a></li>';
              $(document).find(toc).append(content);
            }

            // Add section code to subnavigation
            var children = $('<nav class="md-nav"><ul class="md-nav__list"></nav></ul>')
            var contenders = $("#" + div_id).nextUntil("h1");
            $.each(contenders, function(idx, contender){
               if( !$(contender).hasClass("noTOC") && ($(contender).is('h2') || $(contender).is('h3')) ) {
                   var contender_id = $(contender).attr('id');
                   var contender_text = $(contender).text().split('¶')[0];
                   var content = '<li class="md-nav__item"><a class="md-nav__link" href="#' + contender_id + '" title="' + contender_text +'">' + contender_text +'</a></li>';
                   children.append(content);
                }
             })
             $("#link_" + div_id).append(children);
        });
        //added 'selected' tag to the first element of toc
        $('.md-nav__link').first().addClass('selected');

        $(window).scroll(function(e){
          // Detect how far are we from the top of the page
          let windowTop = $(this).scrollTop();
          // Loop through every navigation menu item
          $('.md-nav__link').each(function (event) {       
              if (windowTop >= $($(this).attr('href')).offset().top - 100) {
              // Remove 'selected' from previously highlighted menu items
              $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
              // Highlight the current menu item by adding 'selected' class
              $(this).addClass('selected');
          }
          if($(window).scrollTop() + $(window).height() > $(document).height() - 10) {
            $('.selected').removeClass('selected');
              $(this).addClass('selected');
          }
        });
      })
      // Smooth scroll to target section when clicking on TOC link
      $('a[href^="#"]').on('click', function(event) {
        event.preventDefault();
        var target = $(this.hash);
        if (target.length) {
          $('html, body').animate({
          scrollTop: target.offset().top - 115
          }, 1000);
        }
      });
    });
</script>
